title: Many of the “Michigan Jewish Dems” Backing Mike Rogers Are Actually Already Republican Supporters, Analysis Finds
author: Drop Site News

_Story by Tom Perkins_

Over 400 alleged Michigan Jewish Democratic and independent voters signed a
[pledge in late August](https://www.mijewsvote.com/) to vote for Republican
U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers, igniting a controversy and generating
questions about whether Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was losing critical
support among a group that typically votes blue by about a 2:1 ratio.

But a Drop Site review of signatories in the "[Michigan Jews Against
Extremism](https://www.mijewsvote.com/)" campaign finds many of the Jewish
community leaders involved have deep ties to the GOP, as well as to pro-Israel
activist groups such as AIPAC. Nearly 50 were involved in a nearly identical
gambit in 2012 that went by the name "Jews for Mitt." Then-President Barack
Obama, the group argued, was so "anti-Israel" that their consciences drove
them to abandon the Democratic Party to support Republican nominee Mitt
Romney.

Among those who signed both the Romney and Rogers pledges are six members of
the Schostaks, a politically powerful family behind a major Michigan
development company. Bobby Schostak, the former head of the Michigan
Republican Party, signed the Jews For Mitt pledge, but this time did not
pretend to be a Democrat--he now serves as the Rogers campaign's finance
chair.

Dozens of signatories either work with the GOP, have served in office as
Republicans, have run as Republicans, or donate to right-wing candidates,
including Donald Trump.

The operation, however, has been extraordinarily effective, garnering enormous
media attention, which frames the group as genuine Democrats who were finally
pushed over the edge by El-Sayed.

Taken together, nearly 90% of the first 430 signatories are either connected
to pro-Israel activist groups, GOP aligned, Jews for Mitt voters, or may not
live in Michigan.

The Michigan Jews campaign appears to be an "astroturf operation" led by AIPAC
and other Republican-affiliated activists, said Jess Newman, a former special
assistant for AIPAC's vice CEO. She now works with the Democratic Socialists
of America.

Many of the top signatories are well-known Jewish community leaders, Newman
added, and the campaign seeks to "create a permission structure to vote for
Rogers" for less politically active Democratic Jews who do not know that most
of these leaders are connected to Republicans, or are Republicans.

"They are using this brazen tactic because they know that people aren't going
to look deeply into it, and some Jewish voters will say 'Oh, I recognize a few
names on this list so I can find a way to hold my nose and vote for the
Republican," Newman said. "The implication is that this is a list of Democrats
who otherwise would vote for Democrats, had a red line not been crossed."

The campaign's website states, "Many of us have been fiercely supportive of
Democratic candidates and principles." But FEC records show many signatories
have donated to GOP candidates, including Trump, Rick Snyder, Kelly Loeffler,
Marco Rubio, Mike Lee, Rick Santorum, the Republican National Congressional
Committee, and PACs that support a wide range of Republican candidates,
including GOP Michigan House Leader Matt Hall.

Among the signatories are current and former leadership for AIPAC, as well as
groups that have led the charge against pro-Palestinian advocates in Michigan
and nationally, including the Jewish Federation, Hillel, and Anti-Defamation
League.

Drop Site did not include in its 90% figure people who simply are connected
with a Jewish communal group, or a synagogue not involved in Israel activism.
However, it did include those in leadership at synagogues Adot Shalom and
Shaarey Zedek, which
[openly](https://www.facebook.com/adatshalomsyn/photos/adat-shalom-synagogue-
goes-to-washington-who-do-you-recognize-from-our-synagogue/1842774949075003/)
[work with AIPAC](https://shaareyzedek.org/connect/israel/m), support the IDF,
and make pro-Israel activism a central component of their mission.

The list's first signer is Adam Kaplan, a Hillel donor, AIPAC donor, former
Jewish Federation committee member, and an
[appointee](https://www.michigan.gov/formergovernors/recent/snyder/press-
releases/2016/06/17/gov--rick-snyder-makes-appointment-to-the-michigan-
council-for-rehabilitation-services?utm_source=chatgpt.com) in the
administration of Republican former Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder.

Some signatories have run for office as Republicans, including Bubba Urdan, a
West Bloomfield resident who [ran for the GOP
nomination](https://patch.com/michigan/westbloomfield/meet-the-candidates-
bubba-urdan?utm_source=chatgpt.com) in the Michigan state house, and has
served on Jewish Federation boards. Urdan did not respond to a request for
comment.

A spokesperson for Michigan Jews Against Extremism said the letter "was not
organized by AIPAC or in coordination with it or any other organization." She
did not address questions about the Republican ties.

The signatories' AIPAC-GOP connections run deep. Among them is David
Handelman, a Mitch McConnell [donor](https://www.city-data.com/elec2/20/elec-
BLOOMFIELD-HILLS-MI-20-part1.html) and former AIPAC Michigan president who
once [organized a Detroit pro-Israel
event](https://digital.bentley.umich.edu/djnews/djn.2007.05.17.001/21) with
the 2002 Iraq War architect and diplomat John Bolton as the featured speaker.

Former [AIPAC national president](https://dawnmena.org/david-victor/) David
Victor still sits on its national board, and donated to Mike Rogers in 2010.
He also [donated
to](https://www.campaignmoney.com/political/contributions/david-
victor.asp?cycle=10) John McCain and GOP Ohio Congress members John Boehner
and Rob Portman, as well as many Democrats.

Max Newman is a metro Detroit attorney and AIPAC activist who also works with
Hillel. Campaign finance [records
show](https://www.opensecrets.org/search?page=2&q=Max+Newman&type=donors) he
donated to Rogers multiple times in the aughts, Rudy Giuliani, the National
Republican Congressional Committee and many Democrats.

Joshua Opperer is the [executive director of AIPAC's National New Leaders
Network](https://www.honigman.com/search?do_site_search=1&page=9&searchtext=2023&section%5B1%5D=1&utm_source=chatgpt.com)
and Jewish Federation of Detroit's [executive
committee](https://jewishdetroit.org/about/leadership/) recently [donated
$10,000](https://www.opensecrets.org/donor-lookup/results?name=Joshua+Opperer)
to AIPAC, and published a Substack article titled, "Fireworks in Rafah," that
includes a picture of Israeli soldiers celebrating Israel's independence day
by lighting off fireworks in Rafah. He has [donated](https://www.city-
data.com/elec2/elec-HUNTINGTON-WOODS-MI.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) to
several Republicans, as well as Democrats.

The 2012 Jews For Mitt [ad
declares](https://www.scribd.com/document/111296878/Romney-Ad) "We are
Michigan Jews. Four years ago many of us voted for Barack Obama. Today we are
voting for Mitt Romney." The ad alleges Obama had "anti-Israel policies," and
claims Mitt Romney would "aggressively combat Muslim extremism" and "fortify
America's crucial relationship with Israel."

Among the 49 people who are a part of both campaigns are the Schostacks,
Urdan, Max Newman, Victor, and Handelman, who are all Republicans or have
donated to Republicans. It includes many other AIPAC activists, like Margo
Woll.

"They are dusting off their old strategy of trying to create a grass-tops
campaign that makes it look like Jewish people in general are not going to
vote for the Democratic nominee," said former Democrat Congress member Andy
Levin, who was defeated in a 2022 election bid by the AIPAC-backed Haley
Stevens in a metro Detroit district. Only about one-third of Michigan Jews are
Republican, Levin said, and he believes most Jews will still vote for El-
Sayed.

The campaign spokesperson told Drop Site, "For some signatories, our concern
is much more personal: as Jews we do not feel safe when political rhetoric
minimizes antisemitism, excuses or contextualizes violence against Jews, or
embraces an agenda we believe is hostile to our community, our safety and our
children's safety."

"We are speaking for ourselves, exercising our right as Michigan voters, and
asking to be heard without being reduced to a political label."

Among those who do not appear to live in Michigan is Hannan Lis, who [told
Detroit ABC affiliate ](https://www.wxyz.com/news/michigan-couple-living-in-
israel-share-experiences-amid-conflict-with-
iran?utm_source=chatgpt.com)_[WXYZ](https://www.wxyz.com/news/michigan-couple-
living-in-israel-share-experiences-amid-conflict-with-
iran?utm_source=chatgpt.com)_ in March that he moved to Israel several years
ago to be closer to his grandkids, and who has been described as an "Israeli
citizen" in older media reports. He was [part
of](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hannanlis?utm_source=chatgpt.com) the Jewish
Federation's board of governors and the AIPAC National Council. Lis told Drop
Site he is a dual citizen who splits time between Israel and Michigan. He is
registered to vote in Michigan.

"The key question here is 'Who speaks for the Jews and who are the Jews?'"
said Levin, a former Michigan synagogue president.

"This idea that these right wing-on-Israel groups are the Jewish people or
they represent the Jewish people is just demonstrably false," Levin added. He
said there is an intense organizing effort in Michigan's Jewish community for
El-Sayed, but the media and the vast amount of attention goes to a
statistically small number of voters who are pledging to cast a ballot for
Rogers.

Levin's father, former Rep. Sandy Levin, 95, who served as the powerful chair
of the House Ways and Means Committee, [made an unusual foray back into
politics](https://www.timesofisrael.com/jewish-democratic-elder-statesman-
sander-levin-backs-abdul-el-sayed-in-michigan-senate-race/) to endorse El-
Sayed this week. On Wednesday, a list of over 600 Michigan Jews pledging to
support El-Sayed was released.

Jewish voters make up about 1% of Michigan's electorate, and right-wing Jewish
voters may represent as little as .3% of voters statewide. The number of
Democrats who may switch is even more miniscule within the context of the
state's electorate. That raises questions about the outsize media attention to
this tiny group of voters, Levin said.

Some on the list, and some Jewish Democrats, genuinely may not be able to vote
for El-Sayed, Jess Newman said. She added that the campaign is "preying on
latent Islamophobia."

"It's about depressing voter turnout for El-Sayed and getting people on the
margins, and if they have to lie to get there, then they will," Newman added.
